[[File:Edward-curves.svg|right|thumb|Edwards curves of equation ''x''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''y''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;1&nbsp;+&nbsp;''d''&nbsp;·''x''<sup>2</sup>·''y''<sup>2</sup> over the real numbers for ''d''&nbsp;=&nbsp;−300 (red), ''d''&nbsp;=&nbsp;−{{radic|8}} (yellow) and ''d''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.9 (blue)]]

In [[mathematics]], the '''Edwards curves''' are a family of [[elliptic curve]]s studied by [[Harold Edwards (mathematician)|Harold Edwards]] in 2007. The concept of elliptic curves over [[finite fields]] is widely used in [[elliptic curve cryptography]]. Applications of Edwards curves to [[cryptography]] were developed by [[Daniel J. Bernstein]] and [[Tanja Lange]]: they pointed out several advantages of the Edwards form in comparison to the more well known [[Weierstrass form]].<ref>{{Citation
| first1=Daniel | last1=Bernstein
| first2=Tanja | last2=Lange
| title=How to design an elliptic-curve signature system | date=3 March 2014 | url=https://blog.cr.yp.to/20140323-ecdsa.html
}}</ref>

==Definition==

The equation of an Edwards curve over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] ''K'' which does not
have [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic 2]] is:

: <math> x^2 + y^2 = 1 + d\ x^2 y^2 \, </math>

for some [[scalar field|scalar]] <math>d\in K\setminus\{0,1\}</math>.
Also the following form with parameters ''c'' and ''d'' is called an Edwards curve:

: <math> x^2 + y^2 = c^2(1 + d\ x^2 y^2) \, </math>

where ''c'',&nbsp;''d''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''K'' with ''cd''(1&nbsp;−&nbsp;''c''<sup>4</sup>·''d'')&nbsp;≠&nbsp;0.

Every Edwards curve is [[birationally equivalent]] to an elliptic curve in [[Montgomery curve|Montgomery form]], and thus admits an [[algebraic group]] law once one chooses a point to serve as a neutral element.  If ''K'' is finite, then a sizeable fraction of all elliptic curves over ''K'' can be written as Edwards curves.
Often elliptic curves in Edwards form are defined having c=1, [[without loss of generality]]. In the following sections, it is assumed that c=1.

==The group law==
(See also [[elliptic curve#The group law|Weierstrass curve group law]])

Every Edwards curve <math>x^2 + y^2 = 1 + dx^2y^2</math> over field ''K'' with characteristic not equal to&nbsp;2 with <math>d \ne 1</math> is birationally equivalent to an elliptic curve over the same field: <math>(1/e)v^2 = u^3 + (4/e - 2)u^2 + u</math>, where <math>e=1-d, u=\frac{1+y}{1-y}, v=\frac{2(1+y)}{x(1-y)}</math> and the point <math>P = (0,1)</math> is mapped to the infinity ''O''. This birational mapping induces a group on any Edwards curve.

===Edwards addition law===

On any elliptic curve the sum of two points is given by a rational expression of the coordinates of the points, although in general one may need to use several formulas to cover all possible pairs. For the Edwards curve, taking the [[identity element|neutral element]] to be the point&nbsp;(0,&nbsp;1), the sum of the points <math>(x_1,y_1)</math> and <math>(x_2,y_2)</math> is given by the formula

:<math> (x_1,y_1) + (x_2,y_2) = \left( \frac{x_1 y_2 + x_2 y_1}{1 + dx_1 x_2 y_1 y_2}, \frac{y_1 y_2 - x_1 x_2}{1 - dx_1 x_2 y_1 y_2} \right) \, </math>

The [[additive inverse|opposite]] of any point <math>(x,y)</math> is <math>(-x,y)</math>. The point <math>(0,-1)</math> has order&nbsp;2, and the points <math>(\pm 1,0)</math> have order&nbsp;4. In particular, an Edwards curve always has a point of order&nbsp;4 with coordinates in ''K''.

If ''d is not a square'' in ''K'' and <math> \{(x_1,y_1), (x_2,y_2)\} \in \{(x,y)|x^2+y^2=1+d x^2 y^2 \}^2</math>, then there are no exceptional points: the denominators <math>1 + dx_{1}x_{2}y_{1}y_{2}</math> and <math>1 - dx_{1}x_{2}y_{1}y_{2}</math> are always nonzero. Therefore, the Edwards addition law is complete when ''d'' is not a square in ''K''. This means that the formulas work for all pairs of input points on the Edwards curve with no exceptions for doubling, no exception for the neutral element, no exception for negatives, etc.<ref name="BernsteinLange">Daniel. J. Bernstein , Tanja Lange, pag. 3, '' Faster addition and doubling on elliptic curves''</ref> In other words, it is defined for all pairs of input points on the Edwards curve over ''K'' and the result gives the sum of the input points.

If ''d is a square'' in ''K'', then the same operation can have exceptional points, i.e. there can be pairs of points <math> (x_1,y_1), (x_2,y_2) \in \{(x,y)|x^2+y^2=1+d x^2 y^2 \} </math> such that one of the denominators becomes zero: either <math>1 + dx_{1}x_{2}y_{1}y_{2} = 0</math> or <math>1 - dx_{1}x_{2}y_{1}y_{2} = 0</math>.

The addition formula above is faster than other unified formulas and has the strong property of completeness, which refers to its property of not requiring exceptions or branches in its computation. One of the attractive features of the Edwards Addition law is that it is strongly ''unified'' i.e. it can also be used to double a point, simplifying protection against [[side-channel attack|side-channel attacks]].<ref name="BernsteinLange"/> The fact that the Edwards Addition law is a non-branching algorithm means that it can avoid leaking timing information related to branching via the amount of power drawn by the computer.

'''Example of addition law ''':

Consider the elliptic curve in the Edwards form with ''d''=2

:<math>{\displaystyle}x^2 + y^2 = 1 + 2 x^2 y^2</math>

and the point <math>P_1=(1,0)</math> on it. It is possible to prove that the sum of ''P''<sub>1</sub> with the neutral element (0,1) gives again P<sub>1</sub>. Indeed, using the formula given above, the coordinates of the point given by this sum are:

:<math>x_3 = \frac{x_1 y_2 + y_1 x_2}{1 + 2x_1 x_2 y_1 y_2} = 1</math>

:<math>y_3 = \frac{y_1 y_2 - x_1 x_2}{1 - 2x_1 x_2 y_1 y_2} = 0</math>

===An analogue on the circle===
[[File:Edwards Curve,Clock group diagram.jpg|300px|right|thumb|Clock group]]
To understand better the concept of "addition" of points on a curve, a nice example is given by the classical [[circle group]]:

take the circle of radius 1

:<math>{\displaystyle}x^2+y^2=1</math>

and consider two points {{math|1=P<sub>1</sub>=(x<sub>1</sub>,y<sub>1</sub>)}}, P<sub>2</sub>=(x<sub>2</sub>,y<sub>2</sub>) on it. Let α<sub>1</sub> and α<sub>2</sub> be the angles such that:

:<math>{\displaystyle}P_{1}=(x_{1},y_{1})=(\sin{\alpha_{1}},\cos{\alpha_{1}})</math>
:<math>{\displaystyle}P_{2}=(x_{2},y_{2})=(\sin{\alpha_{2}},\cos{\alpha_{2}})</math>

The sum of P<sub>1</sub> and P<sub>2</sub> is, thus, given by the sum of "their angles". That is, the point P<sub>3</sub>=P<sub>1</sub>+P<sub>2</sub> is a point on the circle with coordinates ({{math|1=x<sub>3</sub>,y<sub>3</sub>}}), where:

:<math>{\displaystyle}x_{3}=\sin({\alpha}_{1}+{\alpha}_{2})=\sin{\alpha}_{1}\cos{\alpha}_{2}+\sin{\alpha}_{2}\cos{\alpha}_{1}=x_{1}y_{2}+x_{2}y_{1}</math>
:<math>{\displaystyle}y_{3}=\cos({\alpha}_{1}+{\alpha}_{2})=\cos{\alpha}_{1}\cos{\alpha}_{2}-\sin{\alpha}_{1}\sin{\alpha}_{2}=y_{1}y_{2}-x_{1}x_{2}.</math>

In this way, the addition formula for points on the circle of radius 1 is:

:<math>{\displaystyle}(x_1,y_1)+(x_2,y_2) = (x_1y_2+x_2y_1,y_1y_2-x_1x_2)</math>.

===Addition on Edwards curves===

[[File:Sum of two points on an Edwards curve.svg|thumb|Sum of two points on the Edwards curve with d = -30]]
[[File:Double Point on Edwards Curve.svg|thumb|Doubling a point on the Edwards curve with d=-30]]
The points on an elliptic curve form an [[abelian group]]: one can add points and take integer multiples of a single point. When an elliptic curve is described by a non-singular [[cubic equation]], then the sum of two points ''P'' and ''Q'', denoted ''P''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''Q'', is directly related to third point of intersection between the curve and the [[Elliptic curve#The group law|line that passes through ''P'' and ''Q'']].

The birational mapping between an Edwards curve and the corresponding cubic elliptic curve maps the straight lines into conic sections<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://eprint.iacr.org/2009/155|title=Faster Computation of the Tate Pairing|author=Christophe Arene |author2=Tanja Lange |author3=Michael Naehrig |author4=Christophe Ritzenthaler|year=2009|accessdate=28 February 2010|bibcode=2009arXiv0904.0854A|arxiv=0904.0854}}</ref> 
<math>Axy + Bx + Cy + D = 0</math>. In other words, for the Edwards curves the three points <math>P</math>, <math>Q</math> and <math>-(P+Q)</math> lie on a [[hyperbola]].

Given two distinct non-identity points <math>P_1=(x_1,y_1), P_2=(x_2,y_2), P_1 \ne P_2</math>, the coefficients of the [[quadratic form]] are (up to scalars):

<math> A = (x_1 - x_2) + (x_{1}y_{2} - x_{2}y_{1})</math>,

<math> B = (x_{2}y_{2} - x_{1}y_{1}) + y_{1}y_{2}(x_{2} - x_{1})</math>,

<math> C = x_{1}x_{2}(y_{1} - y_{2}), D = C</math>

In the case of doubling a point <math>P=(x,y)</math> the inverse point <math>-2P</math> lies on the conic that touches the curve at the point <math>P</math>. The coefficients of the quadratic form that defines the conic are (up to scalars{{Clarify|date=December 2021}}):

<math> A = dx^2y - 1</math>,

<math> B = y - x^2</math>,

<math> C = x(1 - y), D = C</math>

==Projective homogeneous coordinates==
In the context of cryptography, [[homogeneous coordinates]] are used to prevent [[elliptic curve cryptography|field inversions]] that appear in the affine formula. To avoid inversions in the original Edwards addition formulas, the curve equation can be written in [[projective space|projective coordinates]] as:

<math>(X^2+Y^2)Z^2=Z^4+dX^2Y^2</math>.

A projective point <math>(X : Y : Z)</math> corresponds to the [[Affine space|affine point]] <math>(X/Z : Y/Z)</math> on the Edwards curve.

The identity element is represented by <math>(0 : 1 : 1 )</math>. The inverse of <math>(X : Y : Z)</math> is <math>(-X : Y : Z)</math>.

The addition formula in homogeneous coordinates is given by: <math>(X_1 : Y_1 : Z_1)+(X_2 : Y_2 : Z_2 )=(X_3 : Y_3 : Z_3 )</math>

where

<math>X_3 = Z_{1}Z_{2}(X_{1}Y_{2} + X_{2}Y_{1})(Z_{1}^{2}Z_{2}^{2} - dX_{1}X_{2}Y_{1}Y_{2})</math>

<math>Y_3 = Z_{1}Z_{2}(Y_{1}Y_{2} - X_{1}X_{2})(Z_{1}^{2}Z_{2}^{2} + dX_{1}X_{2}Y_{1}Y_{2})</math>

<math>Z_3 = (Z_{1}^{2}Z_{2}^{2} - dX_{1}X_{2}Y_{1}Y_{2})(Z_{1}^{2}Z_{2}^{2} + dX_{1}X_{2}Y_{1}Y_{2})</math>

===Algorithm===

Addition of two points on the Edwards curve could be computed more efficiently<ref name="Twisted Edwards curves revisited">Huseyin Hisil, Kenneth Koon-Ho Wong, Gary Carter, and Ed Dawson. Twisted Edwards curves revisited. In ASIACRYPT
2008, pages 326–343, 2008</ref> in the extended Edwards form <math>(X:Y:Z:T)</math>, where <math>T=XY/Z</math>:

<math>(X_3:Y_3:Z_3:T_3) = (X_1:Y_1:Z_1:T_1) + (X_2:Y_2:Z_2:T_2)</math>

<math>A = X_{1}X_{2}; B = Y_{1}Y_{2}; C = dT_{1}T_{2}; D = Z_{1}Z_{2};</math>

<math>E = (X_{1} + Y_{1})(X_{2} + Y_{2}) - A - B; F = D - C; G = D + C; H = B - A;</math>

<math>X_3 = E \cdot F; Y_3 = G \cdot H; Z_3 = F \cdot G; T_3 = E \cdot H;</math>

==Doubling==
''Doubling'' can be performed with exactly the same formula as addition. Doubling refers to the case in which the inputs (''x''<sub>1</sub>,&nbsp;''y''<sub>1</sub>) and (''x''<sub>2</sub>,&nbsp;''y''<sub>2</sub>) are equal.

Doubling a point <math>P=(x,y)</math>: 

<math>
\begin{align}
(x,y)+(x,y) & = \left( \frac{2xy}{1+dx^2y^2}, \frac{y^2-x^2}{1-dx^2y^2} \right) \\[6pt]
& = \left( \frac{2xy}{x^2+y^2}, \frac{y^2-x^2}{2-x^2-y^2} \right)
\end{align}
</math>

The denominators were simplified based on the curve equation <math>x^2 + y^2 = 1 + dx^2y^2</math>. Further speedup is achieved by computing <math>2xy</math> as <math>(x + y)^2 - x^2 - y^2</math>. This reduces the cost of doubling in homomorphic coordinates to 3'''M'''&nbsp;+&nbsp;4'''S'''&nbsp;+&nbsp;3'''C'''&nbsp;+&nbsp;6'''a''', while general addition costs 10'''M'''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1'''S'''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1'''C'''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1'''D'''&nbsp;+&nbsp;7'''a'''. Here '''M''' is field multiplications, '''S''' is field squarings, '''D''' is the cost of multiplying by the curve parameter ''d'', and '''a''' is field addition.

;Example of doubling

As in the previous example for the addition law, consider the Edwards curve with d=2:

<math>x^2 + y^2 = 1 + 2 x^2 y^2</math>

and the point <math>P=(1,0)</math>. The coordinates of the point <math>P_2 = 2P_1</math> are:

<math>x_2 = \frac{2xy}{x^2 + y^2} = 0</math>

<math>y_2 = \frac{y^2-x^2}{2 - (x^2 + y^2)} = -1</math>

The point obtained from doubling ''P'' is thus <math>P_2=(0,-1)</math>.

==Mixed addition==
Mixed addition is the case when Z<sub>2</sub> is known to be 1. In such a case A=Z<sub>1</sub><sup>.</sup>Z<sub>2</sub> can be eliminated and the total cost reduces to 9'''M'''+1'''S'''+1'''C'''+1'''D'''+7'''a'''

===Algorithm===
A= Z<sub>1</sub><sup>.</sup>Z<sub>2</sub> // in other words, A= Z<sub>1</sub>

B= Z<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup>

C=X<sub>1</sub>.X<sub>2</sub>

D=Y<sub>1</sub><sup>.</sup>Y<sub>2</sub>

E=d<sup>.</sup>C<sup>.</sup>D

F=B-E

G=B+E

X<sub>3</sub>= A<sup>.</sup>F((X<sub>I</sub>+Y<sub>1</sub>)<sup>.</sup>(X<sub>2</sub>+Y<sub>2</sub>)-C-D)

Y<sub>3</sub>= A<sup>.</sup>G<sup>.</sup>(D-C)

Z<sub>3</sub>=C<sup>.</sup>F<sup>.</sup>G

==Tripling==
''Tripling'' can be done by first doubling the point and then adding the result to itself. By applying the curve equation as in doubling, we obtain

: <math> 3(x_1,y_1) = \left( \frac{(x_1^2+ y_1^2)^2 - (2 y_1)^2}{4(x_1^2-1)x_1^2 - (x_1^2-y_1^2)^2}x_1, \frac{(x_1^2+ y_1^2)^2 - (2x_1)^2}{-4(y_1^2-1)y_1^2+(x_1^2-y_1^2)^2}y_1 \right). \, </math>

There are two sets of formulas for this operation in standard Edwards coordinates. The first one costs 9'''M'''&nbsp;+&nbsp;4'''S''' while the second needs 7'''M'''&nbsp;+&nbsp;7'''S'''. If the '''S/M''' ratio is very small, specifically below 2/3, then the second set is better while for larger ratios the first one is to be preferred.<ref>Bernstein et al.,  Optimizing Double-Base Elliptic curve single-scalar Multiplication</ref>
Using the addition and doubling formulas (as mentioned above) the point (''X''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;''Y''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;''Z''<sub>1</sub>) is symbolically computed as 3(''X''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;''Y''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;''Z''<sub>1</sub>) and compared with (''X''<sub>3</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;''Y''<sub>3</sub>&nbsp;:&nbsp;''Z''<sub>3</sub>)

;Example of tripling

Giving the Edwards curve with d=2, and the point P<sub>1</sub>=(1,0), the point 3P<sub>1</sub> has coordinates:

<math>x_3 = \frac{(x_1^2+ y_1^2)^2 - (2 y_1)^2}{4(x_1^2-1)x_1^2 - (x_1^2-y_1^2)^2}x_1 = -1</math>

<math>y_3 = \frac{(x_1^2+ y_1^2)^2 - 2(x_1 )^2}{-4 (y_1^2-1)y_1^2+(x_1^2-y_1^2)^2}y_1 = 0</math>

So, {{math|1=3P<sub>1</sub>=(-1,0)=P-<sub>1</sub>}}. This result can also be found considering the doubling example: 2P<sub>1</sub>=(0,1), so 3P<sub>1</sub> = 2P<sub>1</sub> + P<sub>1</sub> = (0,-1) + P<sub>1</sub> = -P<sub>1</sub>.

;Algorithm

<code>A=X<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup></code>

<code>B=Y<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup></code>

<code>C=(2Z<sub>1</sub>)<sup>2</sup></code>

<code>D=A+B</code>

<code>E=D<sup>2</sup></code>

<code>F=2D.(A-B)</code>

<code>G=E-B.C</code>

<code>H=E-A.C</code>

<code>I=F+H</code>

<code>J=F-G</code>

<code>X<sub>3</sub>=G.J.X1</code>

<code>Y<sub>3</sub>=H.I.Y1</code>

<code>Z<sub>3</sub>=I.J.Z1</code>

This formula costs 9'''M'''&nbsp;+&nbsp;4'''S'''

==Inverted Edwards coordinates==
Bernstein and Lange introduced an even faster coordinate system for elliptic curves called the ''Inverted Edward coordinates''<ref>Daniel J.Bernstein. Tanja Lange, pag.2,'' Inverted Edward coordinates''</ref> in which the coordinates (''X''&nbsp;:&nbsp;''Y''&nbsp;:&nbsp;''Z'') satisfy the curve (''X''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''Y''<sup>2</sup>)''Z''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;(''dZ''<sup>4</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''X''<sup>2</sup>''Y''<sup>2</sup>) and corresponds
to the affine point (''Z''/''X'',&nbsp;''Z''/''Y'') on the Edwards curve ''x''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''y''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;1&nbsp;+&nbsp;''dx''<sup>2</sup>''y''<sup>2</sup> with XYZ&nbsp;≠&nbsp;0.

'''Inverted Edwards coordinates''', unlike standard Edwards coordinates, do not have complete addition formulas: some points, such as the neutral element, must be handled separately. But the addition formulas still have the advantage of strong unification: they can be used without change to double a point.

For more information about operations with these coordinates see http://hyperelliptic.org/EFD/g1p/auto-edwards-inverted.html

==Extended Coordinates for Edward Curves==
There is another coordinates system with which an Edwards curve can be represented. These new coordinates are called '''extended coordinates'''<ref>H. Hisil, K. K. Wong, G. Carter, E. Dawson ''Faster group operations on elliptic curves''</ref> and are even faster than inverted coordinates.  For more information about the time-cost required in the operations with these coordinates see:
http://hyperelliptic.org/EFD/g1p/auto-edwards.html
